blocks.text: Melissa Auf der Maur: A Bass and a Nikon

Bassist for Hole and later the Smashing Pumpkins, the Montreal-born musician brings more than two hundred photographs from the heart of the grunge years to Toronto. An intimate, searing archive of the last analogue decade.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Melissa Auf der Maur .

When she joined Hole in the summer of 1994, the bassist and photographer Melissa Auf der Maur had one unusual clause written into her contract. A roll of 35mm film was to be waiting for her backstage at every show. Billy Corgan, of the Smashing Pumpkins, had recommended her to Courtney Love. Their album Live Through This had hit stores four days after Kurt Cobain, Love’s husband and Nirvana’s founder, was found dead. Kristen Pfaff, whose place on bass she took, had died of an overdose. She was stepping into a band in mourning.

Born in Montreal in 1972, she had been taking photographs since the age of thirteen, and found behind the lens, and in the darkroom, a shelter for her shyness. At Concordia University, in her home city, her professor Raymonde April, a celebrated Quebec photographer, introduced her to Francesca Woodman, the American who made herself her own subject, her body dissolved by the long exposure, in rooms left to ruin.

Melissa Auf der Maur turned Hole down at first, meaning to begin a master’s in photography. Then she changed her mind. “I remember being on Canal Street and asking for the most durable point-and-shoot Nikon,” she told The New Yorker. “I knew I was on assignment.” Press photographers are allowed the first three songs from the pit and nothing more. Nobody was timing her. With a self-timer and a cable release, she caught herself mid-song. With the Smashing Pumpkins, she would go on to mount the camera on her amplifier.

The photographs in “My ’90s Rock Photographs” breathe the camaraderie of the road. The band poses at a dressing-room mirror, above a catering table strewn with paper cups and coffee pots. The flash bursts in the glass, and Courtney Love, in an ivory slip, stares the lens down. Elsewhere she pedals barefoot on a bicycle down an empty concrete corridor. Against the barriers, teenage girls with damp hair press together, all smiles. Thirty years have passed. And with them, a whole generation is looking back over Melissa Auf der Maur’s shoulder. generation is looking back over her shoulder.
“My ’90s Rock Photographs” runs through June 6, 2027, at the Art Gallery of Ontario , Toronto.
The book My ’90s Rock Photographs is published by DelMonico Books with the museum, 240 pages, $49.95.
